summary: Summarizes the requirements for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting protocols for network access, as criteria for evaluating candidates. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a scorecard for judging systems that let people onto a network, check permissions, and keep records.

subtitle: A scorecard of requirements for judging AAA protocols that control access to networks.

tldr.problem: Several working groups needed an authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) protocol for network access, and each had its own list of requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The memo merges requirements from NASREQ, ROAMOPS, Mobile IP and TIA 45.6 into tables, one each for general, authentication, authorization and accounting needs, marking each as MUST, SHOULD, MAY and so on per source.
tldr.outcome: Protocol submissions are judged against the tables, and may be unconditionally compliant or conditionally compliant. The memo itself defines no protocol.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Millions of users, tens of thousands of simultaneous requests

today: RFC 2989 is an Informational requirements document, and the unit metadata shows it neither obsoleted nor updated. It defines no protocol, only criteria for evaluating submissions.

sections.title: Purpose and How Compliance Works
sections.content:
This memo summarizes AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) protocol requirements for network access. Inputs came from the NASREQ, ROAMOPS and MOBILEIP working groups and from TIA 45.6. Requirements are separated into authentication, authorization and accounting, and the detail stays in the original documents.

The requirement words (MUST, SHOULD, MAY and their negatives) describe capabilities that a protocol must offer, not what traffic must do. Requiring support for confidentiality is not the same as requiring that all traffic be encrypted; the protocol documents decide what is required, recommended or optional.

A submission that fails any MUST or MUST NOT for a capability it implements is not compliant. One that meets all MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and SHOULD NOT items is unconditionally compliant. One that meets all MUST and MUST NOT items but not every SHOULD or SHOULD NOT is conditionally compliant.
sections.eli5: Think of a checklist for a school club. Missing a must-have means you cannot join. Meeting every should-have as well earns top marks.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The memo defines the cast of a roaming AAA system. A client wants service from an attendant within an administrative domain. A proxy acts as a server toward the requester and as a client when it forwards the request. A transparent proxy does not add, delete or modify attributes. A local proxy sits in the same domain as the network device that issued the request and typically enforces local policy.

A broker is in a different administrative domain from both the home AAA server and the local ISP. A proxy broker forwards all AAA messages between the local ISP and the home domain. A routing broker is not in the message path; it returns the information needed to contact the home AAA server directly, and may also act as a Certificate Authority.

Two security models are defined. Hop-by-hop means each direct pair of peers in a proxy network shares a security association and the security information does not traverse a AAA entity. End-to-end means security information can be validated even after intermediate nodes such as proxies and brokers process the message. The memo also defines the Network Access Identifier (NAI), real-time accounting, session records, and inter-domain versus intra-domain accounting.
sections.eli5: Some helpers pass a note along, some only point to where the answer lives, and the people in the middle may or may not be allowed to change it.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
Each requirement in the tables is marked M (MUST), S (SHOULD), O (MAY), N (MUST NOT) or B (SHOULD NOT) for NASREQ, ROAMOPS and Mobile IP. The general table covers scalability (millions of users and tens of thousands of simultaneous requests), fail-over to a backup server, mutual authentication of AAA client and server, transmission level security, and object-level confidentiality and integrity.

Transmission level security is the hop-by-hop model, removed when a AAA entity processes the message. Object-level security protects one or more attributes so that only the target entity can decrypt them and no intermediate server can modify them. The protocol must also carry certificates, provide reliable transport with retransmission and fail-over, run over IPv4 and be able to carry service-specific attributes defined by other groups.

One note says the protocol MUST allow communication to be secured, yet MUST also allow an underlying service such as IP Security to be used, in which case its own security MUST NOT be required.
sections.eli5: The general rules say the system must handle a huge crowd, switch to a spare computer if one breaks, and keep messages private and untampered.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization Requirements
sections.content:
For authentication, the protocol MUST allow Network Access Identifiers to identify users and devices, MUST transport CHAP information, and MUST carry Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) payloads, including mechanisms that need more than one round trip. It must also securely transport clear-text passwords (PAP), protecting them in transit and from disclosure to proxies, even though PAP is called deprecated. Re-authentication must be possible on demand, triggered by the user, the access device or a home or visited AAA server. Authorization without credentials, by identification or assertion only, must be supported.

For authorization, the protocol MUST let a server give a static or dynamic IPv4 or IPv6 address, be compatible enough with the RADIUS attribute base that a server could speak both or translate, and support a reject capability. It must support re-authorization on demand, access rules such as session expirations, idle timeouts, packet filters, static routes and QoS parameters, state reconciliation after outages, and unsolicited disconnect so a server can end an active session.
sections.eli5: The system must accept several ways of showing who you are, be able to ask again later, and be able to hand out an address, set limits, or kick a guest out.

sections.title: Accounting and Mobile IP Requirements
sections.content:
Accounting requirements include real-time accounting, which means reporting synchronously with events with a time window typically on the order of seconds. Other items are compact encoding (accounting data MUST NOT be bloated), extensible accounting records, batch accounting (buffering records and sending them together later), guaranteed delivery through an application layer acknowledgment, accounting time stamps, and dynamic accounting, where a single session can have multiple records.

Mobile IP adds three needs: encoding of Mobile IP registration messages, a protocol that is firewall friendly (so a home agent AAA server behind a firewall can still be reached), and allocation of a local home agent.

The memo has no security concerns of its own, because it is a requirements document. It also creates no new IANA number spaces.
sections.eli5: Counting what each guest used must be fast, tidy and never lost, and the rules include a few extras for devices that move between networks.
